Abolition

/ab-uh-LISH-un/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Abolition means the act of formally putting an end to a system, practice, or law.

Parliament's vote for the abolition of debtors' prisons meant that no one could be locked up simply for owing money.

Worked Example

In the mill towns of Ardenia, children as young as nine worked twelve-hour shifts beside dangerous machines. Reformers spent years documenting the injuries and the lost schooling, publishing reports that shocked the public. Newspapers took up the cause, and lawmakers finally passed the Factory Act. The abolition of child labor closed that chapter of Ardenia's history for good.

Formally ending the entire practice of child labor through law is abolition, the official termination of a system or practice.

How Abolition Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

elimination

elimination: the complete removal of something

termination

termination: the act of bringing something to an end

Antonyms

preservation

preservation: keeping something in existence

continuation

continuation: allowing something to go on

How Strong Is It? — restriction → abolition → eradication

restriction vs. abolition

restriction vs. abolition: A restriction limits a practice but lets it continue, while abolition ends the practice formally and completely.

eradication vs. abolition

eradication vs. abolition: Abolition formally ends a law or system, while eradication wipes something out so thoroughly that no trace of it remains.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — aboli

Root — aboli: from Latin abolere, to destroy, to do away with

Suffix — -tion

Suffix — -tion: the act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin abolere, meaning to destroy or do away with. In English the root survives almost entirely through this one word family, most visibly in the common verb abolish.

Use the root in a new word: abolish

Use the root in a new word: abolish: The senators voted to abolish the outdated tax, ending it for good.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, historical and legal register

Use abolition for formally ending an institution, practice, or law, as in the abolition of an unjust statute. Related word: abolition targets ending the unjust SYSTEM or law itself, while emancipation focuses on the freedom granted to the people affected by it.
